A Tissue Virus Microenvironment with Activated Stress Responses Underlies Durable SIV Persistence
summary: HIV persistence during suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) remains a central barrier to cure, with the majority of reservoirs residing in gut-associated lymphoid tissues (GALT). Here, we define a spatially organized viral microenvironment (VME) that sustains reservoir durability and governs early viral rebound by comparing animals initiating ART early after infection (transient reservoirs) versus late (persistent reservoirs). Using immunoPET/CT-guided sampling of SIV-infected rhesus macaques combined with spatial transcriptomics, we interrogated tissue sites of viral production during the eclipse phase following analytical treatment interruption (ATI). Our results revealed that viral rebound from persistent reservoirs arises from discrete, transcriptionally active foci enriched in the mucosa lining the gut lumen. Eclipse phase persistent reservoirs were characterized by increased proviral burden and a distinct tissue state marked by activation of stress-response, metabolic, mitochondrial, and cell cycle programs coupled to repression of cytoplasmic translation and increased cellular senescence. These features co-occurred with immunosuppressive cellular architectures resembling tertiary lymphoid structures enriched for Treg cells, innate lymphoid cells, and mast cells, regulated by Treg-centered cell-cell interaction networks. In contrast, transient reservoirs displayed enhanced translational and metabolic activity and were embedded within immune-active environments enriched for CD8+ T cells, Th17, Tfh, and activated CD4+ T cells. Machine learning identified stress adaptation, hypoxia, metabolic rewiring, and cytoskeletal remodeling pathways as dominant predictors of viral density within persistent VMEs, with strong convergence on programs observed in tumor microenvironments (TME). Orthogonal validation confirmed activation of the integrated stress response (ISR) at sites of viral production in concurrence with results of immunofluorescent microscopy revealing SIV gag expression in two populations primarily in the mucosa, differentiated by the phosphorylation of eIF2alpha. Together, these findings establish the VME as a critical determinant of reservoir persistence, integrating immune regulation, tissue remodeling, and translational control to enable viral survival. This framework suggests that effective HIV cure strategies will require coordinated disruption of VME-supportive functions in addition to targeting infected cells.

title: Title: Unilateral loss of tyrosine hydroxylase in adult midbrain dopaminergic neurons reveals reduction to neuregulin1 in rat model of acute dopaminergic dysfunction
summary: Dopamine, produced primarily in the midbrain, is required for movement and reward-based signaling all throughout life. Loss of dopaminergic function can result in changes to motor systems, mood, motivation, and cognition. Dopaminergic cell death or dopaminergic hypofunction are implicated in a variety of diseases including synucleinopathies, neuropsychiatric disorders, and substance use disorders. Loss of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and subsequent dysregulation of dopamine signaling in striatum are implicated to varying degrees in all synucleinopathies. By the time patients present with motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease, the most common synucleinopathy, >30% of DANs are lost in the SNpc because of ongoing degeneration for years prior to diagnosis. Studying the early consequences of dopamine loss is critical to understanding mechanisms of dopamine depletion disease progression and identifying biomarkers for earlier diagnosis so that effective treatment can ensue. Here, we created a model of dopamine loss in adult rats to study early transcriptional changes following loss of dopamine synthesis. We used CRISPR to knock out tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine synthesis, in the adult rat midbrain through injection of Th guide RNAs into transgenic rats expressing Cas9 nuclease specifically in dopamine transporter positive neurons and performed single nucleus RNA sequencing on midbrain and dorsal striatal tissue. Two weeks after injection, we measured a 90% loss of TH and dopamine in the midbrain, but striatal TH and dopamine were unaffected. Despite preceding striatal dopamine loss, our data identified alterations to genes involved in synaptic signaling, organization, and function in both midbrain and striatal neurons. We found the neurotrophic factor, neuregulin1, to be significantly reduced in dopaminergic neurons, which may account for transcriptional changes in surrounding cells that precede detectable reductions to striatal dopamine. These data establish a new rat model of adult TH loss and identify early transcriptional consequences of dopamine loss in the adult midbrain after normal development, providing potential biomarkers for early-stage dopamine loss in PD, synucleinopathies and related disorders of dopamine depletion.

title: THE BILE ACID RECEPTOR TGR5 MODULATES HIPPOCAMPAL NEURAL STEM CELL STATE AND AGEING
summary: Ageing locks hippocampal neural stem cells (NSCs) into deeper quiescence and inflammation-driven senescence, which are also associated with impaired cognition. The bile-acid receptor TGR5, a member class I G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), is expressed in cultured hippocampal NSCs and in SOX2-positive cells of the adult sub granular zone, yet its role in NSC homeostasis is unknown. In this study we show that TGR5 selective agonist, TC-G 1005, expanded the NSC pool without forcing neuronal differentiation. Primary NSCs treatment with TC-G 1005 increased BrdU incorporation and PCNA in a concentration-dependent manner, and both responses were lost after TGR5 knockdown. TGR5 agonism in differentiating cultures increased nestin, left doublecortin (DCX) unchanged and suppressed MAP2 expression, preserving stemness rather than neuronal commitment. The agonist also released BMP4-imposed quiescence, lowering FOXO3a and restoring phospho-EGFR and ASCL1, and reopened autophagic flux, with less p62 and LC3-II, fewer LAMP2 puncta and more Beclin-1. Furthermore, activation of TGR5 suppressed IL-6 induced p53 and p16 expression, restored proliferation and contracted the inflammatory transcriptome by more than 90%, including Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b and Cdk6. In 18-month-old mice, brain-penetrant TC-G 1005 (5 mg/kg, subcutaneously, twice daily for 28 days) expanded SOX2-positive and proliferating NSCs, reduced p16, recovered ASCL1 and improved spatial memory, without changing locomotion or generating DCX-positive neurons. Dentate gyrus-restricted TGR5 knockdown abolished these cellular effects and the rescue of spatial and social discrimination. Hippocampal proteomic analysis revealed that TC-G 1005 treated aged mice occupied an intermediate, partially rejuvenated position between young and aged proteomes, with 86 proteins shared between ageing- and treatment-responsive sets, and mitochondrial and complement C1q modules shifted toward youthful levels. TGR5 activation therefore relieves both quiescence and senescence in the aged neurogenic niche without driving neuronal differentiation. Collectively, these results suggest that TGR5 could be targeted to preserve cognition in ageing by rejuvenating the hippocampal stem-cell niche.
